description:
ANKA — We're building a similarity engine that scans Earth with open NASA data to find overlooked regions resembling the Moon and Mars. We validate it against known analogs like the Atacama and Haughton Crater, then surface the unrecognized ones. Python, data analysis, interactive maps.

Looking for: Python/data analysis, GIS or map visualization, graphic design, presentation, English writing. Geology interest a plus, not required.
summary:
Analog sites let mission teams test hardware and crews before they fly, but the ones in use today were found by expedition and habit, not by searching the planet. TerraAnalog scores all 808,053 land cells on Earth against four Moon and Mars environments, using NASA MODIS surface temperature and vegetation, then checks itself against 31 established analog sites before proposing anything new.

That check produced our main finding. The trait real Mars analogs share most is the day-night swing of the ground surface, more than dryness. And established Mars desert analogs are systematically warmer than ordinary land, while Mars averages about -63 C. Ranked by Mars physics instead of practice, the leading overlooked candidates are cold, hyperarid deserts in western Tibet and Xinjiang, stable under 300 random reweightings.

In our own country, one place leads every profile: the Karapinar basin in Konya, beside the Meke Maar. It is the barest ground in Turkiye, in the top 10% of all land on Earth for the lunar mare profile, and a young volcanic field of maars and cinder cones. We found no study that uses it as a planetary analog.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

TerraAnalog searches every land cell on Earth (about 18 km each) for environments that can stand in for four targets: the Martian mid-latitude desert, Martian polar ground ice, the lunar equatorial mare and the lunar south pole. For each target it shows a global map, a ranked list of overlooked candidate regions, and, for every candidate, which parts of the analogy hold and which break. It also shows how well the method recognises the analog sites scientists already use.

HOW IT WORKS

Earth cannot reach lunar or Martian values: lunar noon is about +127 C, lunar night about -173 C, Mars about -63 C at 6 hPa. So we never match absolute numbers. Planetary conditions set a direction for each dimension (drier, barer, colder, larger day-night swing), and each cell is scored on how far along that direction it sits among Earth's own land.

Data per cell:

- NASA MODIS Aqua land surface temperature, monthly day (13:30) and night (01:30), 2020-2024: mean surface temperature, day-night swing, coldest night, yearly range.

- NASA MODIS Terra NDVI, monthly, 2020-2024: the greenest month, so a desert that blooms after rain does not count as bare.

- WorldClim 2.1 rainfall and seasonality; elevation (NASA SRTM-derived), converted to surface pressure; terrain roughness.

NASA Earth Observations (NEO) shut down in September 2026, and the science archives need a login. So we read MODIS from NASA GIBS, which serves the products as images and publishes the colour table behind each one. Every colour stands for one 0.6 K or 0.01 NDVI interval, so decoding the images recovers the data. All 180 monthly images decoded with every pixel matched.

Scoring: each variable becomes its rank among all land cells; closeness to the target rank is scaled to the furthest reachable value; the score is the weighted mean. Candidates are picked 400 km apart, excluding the 31 established sites (300 km radius) and the Antarctic and Greenland ice sheets.

VALIDATION

We built a list of 31 established analog sites, each with a published reference, and tagged each by why it was chosen: environment, geology, or operations. Each is scored at its nearest land cell. The measure is ROC AUC against 50,000 random land cells (0.5 = chance), with bootstrap 95% intervals, compared with rainfall alone.

- Mars polar: AUC 0.80 (0.71-0.93), n=4; rainfall alone 0.76.

- Moon south polar: AUC 0.81 (0.76-0.87), n=3; rainfall alone 0.77.

- Mars desert, environment sites: AUC 0.66 (0.53-0.79), n=8. Rainfall alone does better: 0.79.

- Sites chosen for geology (Ries, Sudbury, Rio Tinto...) score at or below chance. Climate cannot see rocks; we report that as a limit.

THE FINDING

Our physics-based Mars desert profile losing to rainfall alone is the most useful result we have. We scored each dimension on its own against the eight Mars desert sites chosen for their environment:

- Day-night surface swing (MODIS): AUC 0.83, the strongest single trait.

- Hyperaridity: 0.79.

- Cold surface: 0.24. Established sites systematically avoid the cold.

Removing one dimension at a time confirms it: dropping temperature lifts the profile from 0.66 to 0.77, and every other dimension holds or adds value. So the profile agrees with practice on every axis but temperature. Field teams go to Death Valley, the Danakil and the Sahara; Mars is cold.

That gap tells us where to look. Ranked by physics, the top candidates are high, hyperarid deserts on the Tibetan Plateau and in Xinjiang. The leaders, in Ngari and Hotan, are below freezing on average, barely vegetated, and swing about 30 C between day and night; none of the top ten averages above 20 C at the surface. Rank the same way but ignore temperature, as practice does (this variant is labelled as derived after seeing the validation), and half of the top ten become hot deserts in the Sahara and the Atacama, all above 27 C.

We tested our own weights: every weight multiplied by a random factor from 0.5 to 1.5, 300 times. The top three Mars desert and lunar mare candidates stay in the top ten in 100% of runs.

A cross-check: Tibesti in Chad ranks in the top 0.01% of land for the lunar mare profile. NASA Earth Observatory already compares its volcano Emi Koussi with the Martian volcano Elysium Mons, on shape alone. Our search finds the same massif from climate and terrain alone.

CASE STUDY: TURKIYE

Inside Turkiye, one cell leads every profile: 37.75 N, 33.75 E, the Karapinar basin, about 12 km from the Meke Maar. Greenest-month NDVI 0.09, the barest ground in the country; a 25 C day-night surface swing; top 10% of all land on Earth for the lunar mare profile. Independently of our data, it is a Quaternary monogenetic volcanic field of cinder cones, maars and lava flows, basaltic to andesitic (Gall et al., 2021, Lithos), an hour from Konya. We found no study that uses it as a lunar or Martian analog. It suits rover slope tests on maar rims, instrument trials on young volcanic surfaces, and field-geology training. Where it breaks: 388 mm of rain a year, lavas only partly basaltic, and farmland in parts of the basin.

Salda Lake, Turkiye's established Mars analog, ranks low in our search, as expected: it was chosen for carbonate mineralogy, which climate data cannot see. The approaches are complementary.

WHAT WENT WRONG, AND WHAT THIS IS NOT

Our first run put every Mars candidate in interior Antarctica, so we now mask the ice sheets. Our first version used air temperature, and its headline list changed when we switched to MODIS surface temperature; we report the current list. The method has no geology layer and works at 18 km, so it yields a shortlist of regions, not landing sites. Earth cannot reproduce gravity, vacuum, radiation or atmospheric chemistry; each profile states this rather than scoring it.

WHY IT MATTERS

Analog campaigns are expensive and slow, and sites are chosen by habit. A reproducible, validated ranking gives planners a defensible shortlist. It also shows a systematic blind spot in current practice: cold deserts. Everything is open: code, results as CSV, and 17 unit tests.

USE OF SUPER INTELLIGENCE (SI)

We relied heavily on an SI coding assistant (Claude, by Anthropic).

- Method: the assistant proposed the core approach (ranking Earth against Earth, scoring dimensions separately, validating against established sites before proposing new ones), the four target environments and their initial weights. The team chose the challenge, directed the work, questioned the results at each step and decided what to keep, including keeping the physics profile after it lost to the rainfall baseline instead of tuning it.

- Code: the assistant wrote the data pipeline, MODIS decoding, scoring, validation, sensitivity analysis, app and tests.

- Research: it read the challenge text and ran web searches to check whether candidate sites already appear in the analog literature.

- Writing: it drafted the README, this text and the demo slides.

Every number comes from running the code on NASA MODIS, WorldClim and the other data listed below; none was generated by the SI tool. All figures are plotted from our own results. No SI-generated images, video or audio are used.
